source.title: Smoothness-Based Derandomization of PAC-Bayes Bounds
source.authors: Alexandre Lemire Paquin; B. Chaib-draa; Philippe Giguère

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own CIFAR-10 results on batch size and test accuracy, including a regularizer and training-time protocols that bear on the large-batch generalization gap.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports bound values and fitted exponents for bounds; those are not rows because they do not measure the test-error or train-test-gap outcomes named in the versions.
record.test_reason: The CIFAR-10 experiments directly compare held-out accuracy across batch sizes and training budgets, testing V5 in a new convolutional architecture with Adam and an optional Jacobian–Hessian regularizer. The width experiments do not establish that the tested widths exceed the width needed to fit the training set.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the empirical observations: JH regularization helps especially where large batches or noisy labels impair performance, and SHEL test error is approximately constant across tested widths. The paper's principal conclusion is broader: smoothness-based PAC-Bayes derandomization isolates a Jensen-gap generalization penalty, whose control introduces score-map Jacobian and Hessian quantities. The practical regularizer is a proxy inspired by these bounds.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use an eight-layer BatchNorm convolutional network and a SHEL network, and test an added Jacobian-Hessian regularizer and variable-epoch protocol. These differ from the original claim's listed architectures and recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, fixed versus variable epoch budget, clean versus noisy labels, learning rate, and regularizer configuration are reported as affecting the outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST SHEL test error remains approximately constant across tested widths, with fitted exponents −0.045 and −0.107.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing width does not increase test error in this fixed-duration erf-network experiment; the relationship to the fitting threshold is unknown.

fits_no_version.finding: At batch 4096 under variable epochs, JH configurations attain 81.19–81.73% accuracy versus 78.84% for the baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effective-weight JH regularizer improves held-out accuracy at this particular large-batch training configuration.

record.problems: The SHEL width and batch-size test-error trends are presented through figures and textual summaries rather than numerical test-error values. The SHEL bound estimates use an effective sample size much larger than the true sample size and are explicitly not PAC guarantees. The practical Jacobian-Hessian regularizer is described as a proxy, not a direct evaluation of the theoretical quantities.
record.rows_left_out: Section 10, Figure 8 compares four regularizer parameterizations; excluded because the excerpted text only reports a qualitative aggregate comparison and it does not establish a result for the listed claim versions. Section 9 reports test-error batch-size exponents and width-related bound exponents, but the batch-size error values are figure-only and the bounds do not measure the claim's test-error outcome.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting compared with natural-label training and chance-level held-out performance on random labels.
Continued test-error reduction after reaching the width needed for zero training error. The study does not establish that its width sweep enters this regime.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization, local connectivity, and initialization from trained convolutional networks.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning.
Language models, identification of a workload-dependent batch threshold, and isolated effects of learning-rate scaling, normalization changes, or warmup. Warmup is used but not ablated.
Dropout addition or removal, small-data behavior, and excessive-dropout underfitting.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, its association with measured train–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples compared with random removal and retraining.

missing.what: Within-batch comparisons of fixed versus variable epochs for baseline and JH models. The text reports benefits in most cases, with an exception for the noisy-label JH model at batch 4096. These comparisons are needed to separate training-budget effects from regularizer effects.
missing.locator: Section 10, second experiment; Figures 6–7; paragraph beginning with the regularizer's larger gains under label noise

missing.what: Clean-data variable-epoch batch-size trends for baseline and JH models, separately from the fixed-epoch trends in R3–R4. The supplied text reports the clean-data deterioration comparison without separating protocols; numerical curves are unavailable.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any listed version. Adaptation results support qualifications already present in V5; they do not independently challenge its fixed-budget statement. The bounds and regularizer do not directly test V7's specific magnitude-aware sharpness correlation. Figure values were not supplied, so no numerical accuracies or curve-specific significance were inferred.

versions.untested_parts: The stated one-hidden-layer ReLU setup, MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 settings, zero training error, and width beyond the interpolation threshold.
Language models and batches defined by a workload-dependent threshold.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measured as perturbation tolerance and compared with other generalization measures.
Removal of memorized examples and retraining.
